summary:
H.R. 2427, the “Stop Disaster Price Gouging Act,” establishes a temporary federal prohibition on price gouging for certain goods and services during a declared major disaster or emergency, enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), States, and private plaintiffs. The operative trigger is a presidential declaration of a major disaster or emergency under section 401 or 501 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5170, 5191). Within the declared area, a person may not, during the specified periods, (1) increase the price as of the day before the declaration by more than 10 percent—for essential consumer goods and services, hotel lodging, and residential rental properties for 30 days, and for repair or reconstruction services for 180 days; or (2) charge a price more than 50 percent greater than the person’s cost for such goods, services, lodging, rental property, or reconstruction services for 30 days after the declaration if the person did not charge that price before the declaration.

The prohibition is subject to specific exceptions: an increase is permitted if it is directly attributable to additional supplier, labor, or materials costs and does not exceed the cost plus the seller’s customary pre-disaster markup by more than 10 percent; if it is directly attributable to tariffs or national trade policies; for hotel or motel rates, if attributable to regularly scheduled seasonal adjustments; or for rental rates, if attributable to amortized repair or addition costs beyond normal maintenance or if the increase was contractually agreed to by the tenant prior to the disaster or emergency.

A violation of the prohibition is treated as a violation of a rule under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)) regarding unfair or deceptive acts or practices. The FTC shall enforce the prohibition using all powers and procedures of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.). Civil penalties are calculated per violation at up to $25,000, but the total liability for all violations resulting from the same or related acts or practices is capped at $25,000. The penalty amounts are subject to annual inflation adjustments based on the Consumer Price Index beginning one year after enactment. Amounts recovered by the FTC are deposited into a fund to assist communities in disaster-affected areas.

State attorneys general (or designated officials) may bring civil actions as parens patriae in state or federal court for injunctive relief, compliance, damages, restitution, or other equitable relief. Prior notice to the FTC is required; the FTC may intervene, be heard, and petition for appeal. State actions are barred during the pendency of a federal action by the FTC or the U.S. Attorney General against the same defendant for the same alleged violation. The bill does not limit States’ own investigative powers.

A private right of action is created: an injured person may sue in state or federal court for injunctive relief, actual monetary damages, or both. For willful violations, the court may award treble damages. A prevailing plaintiff is entitled to costs and reasonable attorney’s fees. Actions must be commenced within two years of discovery or reasonable opportunity to discover the violation. The private remedy is nonexclusive.

The bill defines “essential consumer goods and services” as goods and services necessary for survival and recovery, enumerating categories including food and drink, emergency supplies, medical supplies, home heating oil, building materials, transportation, freight, storage, and motor fuels. No provision appropriates funds; the Act takes effect upon enactment and does not preempt any non-conflicting State law.
